title: Peleus et Thetis
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Proteus has prophesied that Thetis will bear a son who will outdo his father, and so Jupiter, though he burns for her himself, gives the marriage up and hands his desire to his grandson Peleus. Peleus comes on her asleep in the cave on a sickle-shaped Haemonian bay that she used to ride to naked on a bridled dolphin, and when entreaty fails he turns to force; she escapes him by becoming a bird, a tree and a tigress. He sacrifices to the sea gods until Proteus tells him how to hold her through every change, and the second attempt succeeds. The son of the prophecy is named in the part's last word.

advisory.lede: This part is a rape: Peleus seizes Thetis while she sleeps, readies force when entreaty fails, and — on the sea-prophet Proteus's instructions — holds her down through every shape she takes until she gives in and he gets her with child.
advisory.more: The Latin does not hurry past any of it. At 238–240 Peleus comes on Thetis as she lies asleep in a cave, and when she resists his entreaties he readies force and winds both arms about her neck; only her changes of shape stop him (241–242). At 251–254 Proteus supplies a method: tie her unaware with snares and a bond that holds, and press her, whatever she turns into, until she takes back the form she had before. At 260–262 Peleus falls on her the moment she comes back to her bed and holds on, and she feels her limbs gripped and her arms dragged apart in opposite directions. At 263–265 she gives in, conceding that he wins only with a god behind him, and he gets her with child. The text is presented unaltered, and both English layers keep the force the Latin carries; nothing here is softened.

sentences.t:
Namque senex Thetidi Proteus “dea” dixerat “undae,
concipe:
sentences.l: For the old man Proteus had said to Thetis, “goddess of the wave, conceive:
sentences.i: For old Proteus had once told Thetis: “Goddess of the water, conceive a child:
sentences.n: The speech is wrapped around the verb that reports it: dea stands before dixerat and undae after it, so the vocative “goddess of the wave” is split in two by “had said”. senex is a noun in apposition, “the old man”. dixerat is pluperfect — this prophecy was delivered before anything else in the part, and it is the reason for everything that follows. concipe is an imperative.

sentences.t:
mater eris iuvenis, qui fortibus annis
acta patris vincet maiorque vocabitur illo.”
sentences.l: you will be the mother of a young man who in his years of strength will conquer his father's deeds and will be called greater than that one.”
sentences.i: you will be mother to a young man who, in his prime, will outdo everything his father did and will be called the greater of the two.”
sentences.n: fortibus annis is an ablative of time, “in his strong years”. vincet is the ordinary verb for conquering, used here of deeds: he will beat his father's achievements. maior is completed by illo, an ablative of comparison, “greater than that man”. The Latin names neither the son nor the father here.

sentences.t:
Ergo, ne quicquam mundus Iove maius haberet,
quamvis haud tepidos sub pectore senserat ignes,
Iuppiter aequoreae Thetidis conubia fugit
in suaque Aeaciden succedere vota nepotem
iussit et amplexus in virginis ire marinae.
sentences.l: Therefore, so that the world should have nothing greater than Jove, although he had felt fires beneath his breast that were not lukewarm, Jupiter fled the marriage of sea-dwelling Thetis, and ordered the son of Aeacus, his grandson, to step into his own prayers and to go into the embraces of the sea maiden.
sentences.i: So, to keep the world from holding anything greater than Jove, Jupiter shunned marriage with Thetis of the sea — though the fire he had felt in his own breast was anything but lukewarm — and told his grandson, the son of Aeacus, to take over the desire he was giving up, and to go to the sea-girl's embrace.
sentences.n: ne quicquam ... haberet is a negative purpose clause giving Jupiter's motive. quamvis is followed by the indicative here — senserat is pluperfect indicative, not subjunctive. haud tepidos is litotes: fires “not lukewarm” means fires very hot indeed, and the English keeps the negative because the Latin has it. in sua vota succedere is “to step into his own prayers”: what Jupiter hands over is the wish itself, and vota returns as the last thing Peleus gets (265). Aeaciden carries the Greek accusative ending -en, and it is the plain object of iussit — not an accusative of respect; nepotem stands in apposition to it. conubia and amplexus are poetic plurals.

sentences.t: Est sinus Haemoniae curvos falcatus in arcus:
sentences.l: There is a bay of Haemonia, sickle-curved into bending arcs:
sentences.i: There is a bay in Haemonia, hooked like a sickle into a long curve:
sentences.n: Est standing first opens a set-piece description of a place: 229–236 give nothing but this bay, its headlands, its shore, the myrtle wood and the cave, and 237 names who used to come there. Haemonia is the poetic name for Thessaly. falcatus is built on falx, a sickle, and curvos in arcus gives the shape again from the other side.

sentences.t:
bracchia procurrunt, ubi, si foret altior unda,
portus erat (summis inductum est aequor harenis);
sentences.l: arms run forward, where, if the water were deeper, there was a harbour (the sea has been drawn over the tops of the sands);
sentences.i: two arms of land run out, and if the water there were deeper it would make a harbour — as it is, the sea lies drawn thin across the surface of the sand;
sentences.n: bracchia, “arms”, are the two headlands. si foret altior unda is the protasis of a contrary-to-fact condition, but the apodosis portus erat stands in the plain imperfect indicative where English wants “there would be a harbour” — the indicative states it flatly, as good as fact. foret is an old form of esset. The parenthesis explains why there is no harbour: the water only lies over the top of the sand, and so is shallow.

sentences.t:
litus habet solidum, quod nec vestigia servet
nec remoretur iter, nec opertum pendeat alga.
sentences.l: it has a firm shore, one that would keep no footprints, nor delay a walk, nor hang covered over with seaweed.
sentences.i: the shore is firm, the sort that holds no footprint, does not drag at your steps, and is not matted over with weed.
sentences.n: servet, remoretur and pendeat are three subjunctives in a relative clause of characteristic: the shore is of the kind that would not do these things, not a particular shore that happens not to. The relative quod has litus as its antecedent, and all three verbs hang from it.

sentences.t:
Myrtea silva subest bicoloribus obsita bacis
et specus in medio (natura factus an arte,
ambiguum, magis arte tamen), quo saepe venire
frenato delphine sedens, Theti, nuda solebas.
sentences.l: A myrtle wood lies below, sown thick with two-coloured berries, and a cave in the middle of it (made by nature or by craft is doubtful — more by craft, though), to which you, Thetis, sitting on a bridled dolphin, often used to come, naked.
sentences.i: Below stands a myrtle wood, studded with berries of two colours, and in the middle of it a cave — nature's work or craft's is hard to say, though it looks more like craft's. There, Thetis, riding a bridled dolphin, you used often to come, naked.
sentences.n: The narrative turns here from description to direct address, and stays there: Theti is a Greek vocative, solebas is second person, and Ovid goes on speaking to Thetis through the next several units (iacebas 238, repugnas 239, venisses 241). natura factus an arte is a double indirect question depending on ambiguum, “which of the two, is doubtful” — and Ovid answers his own question in the next three words. sedens frenato delphine uses a bare ablative where English needs “on”; delphine is the ablative of the Greek noun delphin. Magnus prints et specus, which leaves the cave without a verb of its own so that subest has to be carried over to it; some editions print est specus, giving it one.

sentences.t:
Illic te Peleus, ut somno vincta iacebas,
occupat:
sentences.l: There Peleus seizes you, as you were lying bound by sleep:
sentences.i: There Peleus falls on you while you lie fast bound in sleep:
sentences.n: occupat is a historic present dropped in among past verbs — it means “seizes”, and the verb is the one used of taking a thing before anyone else can. ut with the indicative iacebas is purely temporal, “as you were lying”, not purpose or result. vincta is a perfect passive participle with somno as the ablative of what binds her.

sentences.t:
et quoniam precibus temptata repugnas,
vim parat, innectens ambobus colla lacertis.
sentences.l: and since, tried with entreaties, you resist, he readies force, winding your neck about with both his arms.
sentences.i: and since you hold out against him when he tries entreaty, he gets ready to use force, locking both arms around your neck.
sentences.n: temptata is a perfect passive participle addressed to Thetis, “you, having been tried with entreaties”; repugnas is present. The order of the two is the point: entreaty first, then vim parat, “he readies force” — vis here is sexual violence, and both English layers keep it as that. colla is a poetic plural for one neck; ambobus lacertis are his two arms.

sentences.t:
Quod nisi venisses variatis saepe figuris
ad solitas artes, auso foret ille potitus.
sentences.l: And if you had not come, with your shapes often changed, to your accustomed arts, he would have got possession of the thing he had dared.
sentences.i: And if you had not fallen back on your usual arts, changing shape again and again, he would have had what he dared to try for.
sentences.n: A past contrary-to-fact condition: pluperfect subjunctive venisses in the protasis, potitus foret in the apodosis, where foret stands for esset. potior takes the ablative, and what it governs here is auso: audeo is semi-deponent, so its perfect participle ausus wears passive endings and carries active force, and the neuter of it stands as a noun for the venture itself — “the thing he had dared”. variatis saepe figuris is an ablative absolute, “with your shapes changed again and again”, which English has to unpack into a clause. Quod opening the sentence is a connecting relative doing the work of “and”.

sentences.t:
Sed modo tu volucris (volucrem tamen ille tenebat),
nunc gravis arbor eras (haerebat in arbore Peleus),
tertia forma fuit maculosae tigridis:
sentences.l: But at one moment you were a bird (a bird, though, was what he was holding), at the next you were a heavy tree (Peleus clung on in the tree), the third shape was a spotted tigress's:
sentences.i: One moment you were a bird — but a bird was what he had hold of; the next a great tree — and Peleus clung on in the tree; the third shape was a spotted tigress:
sentences.n: Each shape is cancelled by the parenthesis that follows it: bird, but he holds the bird; tree, and he holds the tree. The verb eras in the second clause has to serve the first as well — tu volucris at 243 has no verb of its own. Both parentheses use the imperfect, tenebat and haerebat, for the holding that keeps going; the third shape is stated with a perfect, fuit, and it is the one that works. modo ... nunc is “at one moment ... at the next”.

sentences.t:
illa
territus Aeacides a corpore bracchia solvit.
sentences.l: frightened by that, the son of Aeacus loosed his arms from her body.
sentences.i: That frightened the son of Aeacus, and he loosed his arms from her body.
sentences.n: illa is the last word of 245 and territus the first of 246: the ablative and the participle that governs it are split across the line-end. illa is the ablative of the thing causing fright, “frightened by that shape”. Aeacides is the Greek nominative of the name that stood as accusative Aeaciden at 227 and will stand as vocative Aeacide at 250.

sentences.t:
Isque deos pelagi vino super aequora fuso
et pecoris fibris et fumo turis adorat,
donec Carpathius medio de gurgite vates
“Aeacide,” dixit, “thalamis potiere petitis!
sentences.l: And he worships the gods of the deep with wine poured out over the waters and with the entrails of a beast and with the smoke of incense, until the Carpathian seer said from the middle of the swell, “Son of Aeacus, you will gain possession of the marriage-bed you have sought!
sentences.i: So he made offering to the sea gods — wine poured out across the water, a beast's entrails, the smoke of incense — until the seer of the Carpathian deep spoke up from mid-water: “Son of Aeacus, the marriage you have asked for will be yours!
sentences.n: Three ablatives stand in a row as the instruments of his worship: wine, entrails, smoke. That parallel is what fixes vino ... fuso as an ablative of means with a participle attached to it, and not an ablative absolute — the wine is the thing he worships with. adorat is another historic present, and donec then takes the perfect dixit. The Carpathian seer goes unnamed while he speaks; 255 identifies him as the Proteus who delivered the prophecy at 221. potiere is potieris, the alternative second-person ending, future of potior with the ablative thalamis petitis; thalamis is a poetic plural.

sentences.t:
Tu modo, cum rigido sopita quiescit in antro,
ignaram laqueis vincloque innecte tenaci.
sentences.l: Only do you, when she lies lulled asleep in the hard cave, bind her, unaware, with nooses and with a bond that holds.
sentences.i: Only this: when she is asleep in the rock cave, tie her while she knows nothing of it, with snares and a bond that will not give.
sentences.n: Tu modo, “only do you”, hands the plan across to Peleus. There is no pronoun for “her” anywhere in 252: the single accusative adjective ignaram supplies both the object and a whole clause, “her, while she knows nothing of it”. innecte is the imperative; laqueis and vinclo tenaci are the ablatives of what he is to use. vinclo is the shortened form of vinculo.

sentences.t:
Nec te decipiat centum mentita figuras,
sed preme, quidquid erit, dum, quod fuit ante, reformet!”
sentences.l: And let her not deceive you, having feigned a hundred shapes, but press her, whatever she will be, until she forms again what she was before!”
sentences.i: Do not let her trick you once she has faked a hundred shapes — hold her down, whatever she turns into, until she makes herself again what she was before!”
sentences.n: mentita is deponent: passive in form, active in sense, and it governs centum figuras as a direct object — “having feigned a hundred shapes”, never “having been feigned”. centum is round rather than counted; the shapes actually named in this part are three (243–245). Nec ... decipiat is a prohibition in the subjunctive, and preme the blunt imperative set against it. dum with the subjunctive reformet is “until she shall form again”, looking forward to a moment not yet reached; its object is the relative clause quod fuit ante.

sentences.t:
Dixerat haec Proteus et condidit aequore vultum
admisitque suos in verba novissima fluctus.
sentences.l: Proteus had said these things and hid his face in the water, and let his own waves in upon his last words.
sentences.i: So Proteus finished, and sank his face beneath the surface, letting his waves close in over his last words.
sentences.n: Dixerat is the pluperfect closing off a speech — “he had said this”, which English does as “when he had spoken”. The same form opened the part at 221, reporting his earlier prophecy. novissima is the superlative of novus in its other sense, “last”, not “newest”. admisit ... in verba is the striking phrase: he does not merely sink, he lets his own water in on top of the words, so that the sea closes over the sound of them.

sentences.t:
Pronus erat Titan inclinatoque tenebat
Hesperium temone fretum, cum pulchra relecto
Nereis ingreditur consueta cubilia saxo.
sentences.l: The Titan was sloping downward and, his pole tilted, was holding to the Hesperian sea, when the beautiful Nereid, the rock traversed again, enters her accustomed bed.
sentences.i: The Sun was low, his chariot-pole tilted as he held his course for the western water, when the lovely daughter of Nereus came back past the rock and entered her usual bed.
sentences.n: Titan is the Sun, and inclinato temone an ablative absolute, “with the chariot-pole tilted”; tenebat with an accusative of place is “was holding his course for”. cum ... ingreditur is the inverted cum: the imperfect clause sets the hour and the cum-clause carries the event, so the present ingreditur, a deponent with active sense, lands as the arrival. Nereis is a Greek nominative, “the daughter of Nereus”; the part does not give her name again until 264. consueta cubilia is a poetic plural for one bed. Magnus prints relecto ... saxo, “the rock traversed again”; some editions print relicto ... ponto, “the sea left behind”, which sends her in from the water instead of past the rock.

sentences.t:
Vix bene virgineos Peleus invaserat artus,
illa novat formas, donec sua membra teneri
sentit et in partes diversas bracchia tendi.
sentences.l: Scarcely well had Peleus fallen upon her maiden limbs — she changes her shapes, until she feels her own limbs being held and her arms being drawn into opposite directions.
sentences.i: Peleus had barely set upon her girl's body when she began changing shape after shape — until she felt her limbs held fast and her arms being pulled apart in opposite directions.
sentences.n: There is no conjunction at all between invaserat and illa novat formas: the asyndeton, together with the jump from pluperfect to present, makes the change instantaneous. sentit then governs two accusative-and-infinitive clauses, and both infinitives are passive — membra teneri, “her limbs to be held”, and bracchia tendi, “her arms to be drawn”. invaserat is a verb of assault, and both English layers keep it as one.

sentences.t:
Tum demum ingemuit, “neque” ait “sine numine vincis”
exhibita estque Thetis.
sentences.l: Then at last she groaned, “and not without a god's power do you win,” she says, and Thetis was shown forth.
sentences.i: Then at last she groaned: “You do not win without a god behind you,” she said — and Thetis stood revealed.
sentences.n: Her surrender is a double negative: neque ... sine numine, “and not without a god's power”, concedes divine help while granting him nothing of his own. The verb is vincis, from the same vinco that Proteus used at 223 of the son who will conquer his father's deeds. ait is parenthetical inside the quotation. In exhibita estque the enclitic -que is attached to the auxiliary est rather than to the participle exhibita, and it joins this clause back to ingemuit.

sentences.t:
Confessam amplectitur heros
et potitur votis ingentique implet Achille.
sentences.l: The hero embraces her now that she has confessed, and gains possession of his prayers and fills her with mighty Achilles.
sentences.i: The hero took her in his arms now that she had owned it, got what he had prayed for, and filled her with huge Achilles.
sentences.n: Confessam is deponent and active in sense — “her, now that she has confessed” — and it is the accusative object of amplectitur, itself deponent. potior closes a chain running through the part: the near miss at 242 (potitus), Proteus's promise at 250 (potiere), and the fact here, potitur votis — and vota was Jupiter's own word at 227 for the desire he handed over. The son foretold at 222–223 is finally named in the part's last word, the ablative Achille, and the Latin says it as bluntly as this: Peleus fills her with him.
